Evaluated on five paradigms across 80 algorithm-and-noise conditions, adaptive selection reaches 95.5% of an oracle that always picks the best technique and significantly outperforms all six fixed strategies (Friedman $\chi^{2}=92.18$, $p\approx1.1\times10^{-17}$; pairwise Wilcoxon $p<4\times10^{-6}$). The learned policy is noise-aware: its favored technique shifts as depolarizing and readout error rise. On noise models from eight real IBM devices, APGEM tracks the oracle almost exactly (99.9% of oracle utility) at a flat cost of roughly $1.3\times10^{4}$ shots from three to eight qubits.

title: MusicFlux: Flexible Conditioning for Text-Guided Music Generation and Editing
authors: Leonardo Boulitreau de Menezes Martins Marques
subjects: Sound (cs.SD); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Signal Processing (eess.SP)
abstract: Music editing transforms existing recordings while preserving their original attributes. Recent approaches adapt pretrained text-to-music models for tasks like inpainting, event insertion, or restoration by conditioning them with context audio. It was recently proposed for image editing to unify generation and editing by treating the source image as in-context information. However, applying this directly to music is computationally expensive due to long audio sequences. In this work, we develop MusicFlux, a text-guided music editor built on an efficient pretrained flow-matching text-to-audio model. We introduce two conditioning approaches that trade off editing performance and computational efficiency. Experiments show that both are competitive with strong baselines, with one achieving better editing quality and the other preserving the original sequence length and substantially improving computational efficiency.

title: Optimal Last-Iterate Bounds for Nonexpansive Stochastic Approximation
subjects: Optimization and Control (math.OC); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Systems and Control (eess.SY)
abstract: We establish last-iterate mean-square residual bounds for nonexpansive stochastic approximation (SA), or stochastic Krasnoselskii-Mann (KM) iterations. In particular, we consider fixed-point mappings that are nonexpansive with respect to the Euclidean norm, and focus on polynomially decaying stepsizes. We study three conditions on the conditional second moment of the noise, and obtain bounds that are optimal up to logarithmic factors in each case. When it scales linearly with the squared residual, the best rate is $O(1/k^{1-\epsilon})$ for any $\epsilon>0$. In this case, for all considered stepsizes, our bounds match those of the noiseless KM iteration. When it is bounded by a constant, the best rate is $O(\log^2 k/\sqrt{k})$. When it scales affinely with the squared norm of the iterate, the best rate is $O(1/k^{1/2-\epsilon})$, and the mean-square residual can diverge if the stepsizes are not square-summable. Thus, unlike for contractive SA, square-summable stepsizes are necessary for nonexpansive SA. We demonstrate how various algorithms with cocoercive maps, such as stochastic gradient descent, linear SA, and learning in cocoercive games, fit into our framework, and how the different noise conditions arise in each of them.

title: Beyond Passive Imitation: On-Policy Mid-Training Distillation for Language Models
abstract: Continual pre-training (CPT) adapts large language models (LLMs) to specialized domains, yet its standard next-token prediction (NTP) objective treats every corpus token as a fixed target, regardless of its utility to the current model. In a controlled study on the same 1B-token mathematical corpus, we observe sharply different outcomes across base models: NTP improves Llama-3.2-3B's performance on mathematical benchmarks but substantially degrades Qwen3-1.7B-Base's performance, indicating that, under a fixed training recipe, the same training sequences can have model-dependent effects. To address this problem, we introduce On-Policy Mid-Training Distillation (OPMD), which reformulates mid-training from offline text imitation into active, query-driven knowledge acquisition. At selected anchor positions, OPMD samples trajectories from the evolving student policy and applies dense token-level reverse-KL rewards from a frozen teacher, training the model on states it actually visits rather than only on ground-truth prefixes. This on-policy objective reduces the training-generation mismatch of teacher-forced NTP. On MATH-500 and Minerva, OPMD improves the Qwen student over its base performance and outperforms the evaluated NTP baseline, which degrades on both benchmarks. OPMD integrates into CPT pipelines without added inference-time overhead and offers a model-aware alternative to passive domain adaptation.

title: Outliers and the Hard-Margin Linear SVM in High-Dimension, Low-Sample-Size Settings
abstract: We study how outliers affect the hard-margin linear support vector machine when the dimension grows while the sample sizes remain fixed. For one-sided contamination, the centered Gram matrix converges to a constant inlier block plus an outlier-diagonal component, and the limiting dual problem has a closed-form solution. All outliers act through one effective distance. This representation yields explicit thresholds for loss of inlier support, margin shrinkage. intercept displacement, and asymptotic misclassification. We then treat contamination in both classes. The limiting intercept is the multiplier of the class-balance constraint, and the two classes pull it in opposite directions. Consequently, at most one class can collapse or be asymptotically misclassified, whereas symmetric contamination leaves the limiting discriminant function unchanged even though the margin shrinks. Seven numerical experiments verify the dual allocation, phase transitions, and discriminant limits.

title: Dual-Space Preconditioning for Variational Inequalities and Root-Finding Problems
abstract: This paper develops a dual-space preconditioning framework for variational inequalities and root-finding problems beyond classical cocoercivity and Lipschitz continuity assumptions. To this end, we introduce both a novel cocoercivity-type condition and a relaxed Lipschitz continuity condition, and derive convergence of deterministic and stochastic methods under these generalized conditions. For isotropic preconditioners, the resulting algorithms can be interpreted as variable-stepsize variants of classical methods, extending recent analyses based on $(L_0, L_1)$-type growth conditions while allowing simpler proofs and larger stepsize ranges. We also show that the framework naturally handles variational inequalities through weak Minty-type arguments. Finally, we study the associated continuous-time dynamics and derive a variational and optimal control interpretation of the preconditioned flow. Overall, the results show that dual-space preconditioning provides a flexible mechanism for designing and analyzing operator methods beyond the standard Euclidean Lipschitz setting.

title: Data Quality Challenges in Multimodal Tourism Recommender Systems
comments: 4 pages. Presented at the DaQuaMRec Workshop, co-located with ACM RecSys 2025
abstract: Modern recommender systems increasingly consider diverse data modalities to enhance model performance. However, the quality of the underlying multimodal data (e.g. data from social media platforms) has received limited attention so far. Focusing on tourism recommendation, we examine real-world challenges encountered when using datasets from Yelp and Instagram. Issues include noise from fake reviews, hallucinated content from LLMs, modality contradictions, and demographic bias. We outline future directions such as quality-aware fusion, structured and controlled LLM-based content generation to reduce hallucinations, and user group differentiation to improve the robustness and reliability of multimodal recommendation systems.

title: On the Spectral Estimation of VARMA Processes
comments: 12 pages, 2 figures with the IEEE Transactions template
subjects: Machine Learning (stat.ML); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Optimization and Control (math.OC)
abstract: We consider the problem of estimating the power spectral density of a Vector-valued Autoregressive Moving-Average (VARMA) process. A well-established approach to accomplishing this task consists of formulating a moment problem that selects the spectral density maximizing an entropy-like index while matching certain moments of the underlying process. However, existing methods assume that the moving-average (MA) component is either fixed or scalar, thereby reducing the class of ARMA models over which the optimal spectral density is sought. In this paper, we propose a new moment problem, based on the notion of transportation entropy, for learning the spectral density of a VARMA process without fixing the MA component or restricting it to be scalar.

title: Gradient Inversion through Linear and Affine Subspace Constraints
abstract: Federated learning enables multiple clients to collaboratively train a machine-learning model without directly sharing their local datasets. However, as prior works have shown, the gradients exchanged during training may reveal sensitive information about client data. Most existing attacks usually optimize dummy inputs to match the true client gradients (Gradient Inversion Attacks), while some attempt to reconstruct them based on the observation that aggregate gradients from a fully connected (FC) layer are a linear combination of its inputs. In this work, we extend this observation by showing that aggregate gradients from an FC layer with the correct scaling are actually an affine combination of its inputs. We evaluate a gradient inversion attack that leverages either known linear-subspace information or its affine-subspace counterpart at each FC layer to improve reconstruction accuracy. Our results show that subspace-based methods can substantially improve reconstruction quality over the chosen baselines in certain settings. We further demonstrate that moderate overestimation of the batch size can generally improve or preserve reconstruction quality, even when the true batch size is unknown. We additionally examine reconstruction under gradient perturbations introduced by a differential privacy (DP) mechanism, providing insight into the effectiveness of the considered formulations under noisy conditions.

title: Specify Privacy Yourself: Assessing Inference-Time Personalized Privacy Preservation Ability of Large Vision-Language Models
comments: Accepted by ACM Multimedia 2025 (Brave New Ideas track)
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computation and Language (cs.CL); Computers and Society (cs.CY); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities but raise significant privacy concerns due to their abilities to infer sensitive personal information from images with high precision. While current LVLMs are relatively well aligned to protect universal privacy, e.g., credit card data, we argue that privacy is inherently personalized and context-dependent. This work pivots towards a novel task: can LVLMs achieve Inference-Time Personalized Privacy Protection (ITP$^3$), allowing users to dynamically specify privacy boundaries through language specifications? To this end, we present SPY-Bench, the first systematic assessment of ITP$^3$ ability, which comprises (1) 32,700 unique samples with image-question pairs and personalized privacy instructions across 67 categories and 24 real-world scenarios, and (2) novel metrics grounded in user specifications and context awareness. Benchmarking the ITP$^3$ ability of 21 SOTA LVLMs, we reveal that: (i) most models, even the top-performing o4-mini, perform poorly, with only $\sim$24% compliance accuracy; (ii) they show quite limited contextual privacy understanding capability. Therefore, we implemented initial ITP$^3$ alignment methods, including a novel Noise Contrastive Alignment variant which achieves 96.88% accuracy while maintaining reasonable general performance. These results mark an initial step towards the ethical deployment of more controllable LVLMs. Code and data are available at this https URL

title: LUMIR: Decoupled Multimodal Representation Learning from Heterogeneous Data for Next-POI Recommendation
comments: 16 pages. Accepted at the DaQuaMRec Workshop, co-located with ACM RecSys 2026
abstract: As multimodal tourism-related information collected from heterogeneous data sources has become increasingly available, learning effective representations has attracted attention for improving recommendation performance. Existing approaches often tightly couple multimodal fusion with the architecture and optimization objective of a specific downstream model, which limits the generality and reusability of the learned representations. To address these limitations, we propose LUMIR, a decoupled multimodal representation learning framework based on contrastive learning. Multimodal information collected from heterogeneous data sources is first semantically unified into a shared textual representation space using large language models (LLMs). An interaction-aware fusion mechanism is then designed to model cross-modal interactions, while sequential signals are incorporated as a structural constraint to guide representation learning. To evaluate the learned representations, experiments are conducted on a multimodal point-of-interest (POI) dataset under the next-POI recommendation setting across multiple sequential recommendation backbones. The results show that LUMIR consistently outperforms existing multimodal fusion baselines in both accuracy-oriented and beyond-accuracy metrics, demonstrating that decoupling representation learning from downstream optimization provides an effective paradigm for learning reusable multimodal representations. The code is publicly available at this https URL.

title: Normalizing Flows for Classical Simulation of Quantum Circuits in Phase Space
abstract: We present a novel framework to learn a representation of quantum circuits based on the phase space formulation of many-body systems. Given that $N$-qubit states can be represented as probability distributions on a smooth $2N$-dimensional manifold, we show how unitary gates can be parameterized as normalizing flows between these distributions, opening a new avenue for quantum circuit simulation using generative models. We evaluate our method on three common families of quantum circuits, and show that its accuracy exceeds that of current state-of-the-art neural network methods for large system sizes.

title: Where Do Vision-Language Models Get Left and Right? Position-Code Counterfactuals in Qwen2.5-VL, Qwen3-VL and InternVL3
comments: 25 pages, 6 figures, 10 tables. Code: this https URL
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
abstract: A vision-language model may take left-right direction from the orientation of image content within patches, its vision transformer's (ViT) position code, or token positions and order in its language model (LLM). Ablations show the ViT code is necessary; we test sufficiency by mirroring only a position code. In Qwen2.5-VL-7B, Qwen3-VL-4B and InternVL3-2B, mirroring ViT width positions reproduces the flipped-image answer on 84.3-93.2% of CV-Bench left-right questions (Qwen2.5-VL-3B: 87.5%, partly a left fallback). With two options, this also counts disruption; a half-grid shift flips most answers too. With the ViT code intact, LLM-side id and token-order mirrors change few left-right answers in all three series (a weak id test in Qwen2.5-VL). In Qwen2.5-VL-7B the effect sits in the global-attention ViT blocks, mostly the last. On What'sUp, flipping content and token order, not the position code, keeps more on/under than left-right answers at the flipped-image answer. Post hoc analyses qualify these results. On CV-Bench items with located objects, random permutations flip 18.9-31.0 points more answers when reversing the objects' order than when keeping it. On What'sUp, in Qwen2.5-VL and Qwen3-VL, the share of the left-right changes made by random permutations that land on the mirror relation is mostly below chance. Counted as returns to the original answer, the What'sUp contrast of support with left-right relations is clear only in InternVL3-2B. Most remaining errors give the same relation whichever object is asked about, suggesting that repair may target relation binding, object localization or use of the reference object.

title: What a CAGE 4 Score Measures: An Audit of a Learned Cyber-Defense Benchmark, Its Reference Defenders, and the Tables Built on Them
comments: 47 pages. Code at this https URL (tag arxiv-v1), data at this https URL
abstract: CAGE Challenge 4 is the benchmark on which learned multi-agent cyber defenders are compared. We reproduce its two reference defenders, KEEP and H-MARL Expert, in a pinned container and show that three things read from it measure less than they are taken to measure. First, the simulator silently discards any action asserted for an agent whose previous action is still running, and charges one point for a discarded Restore as for one that runs. The documented observation does not expose the busy flag. Both reference defenders read it in their own wrappers, and switching that check off at evaluation costs KEEP's released policy 99.58 points per episode and H-MARL's 145.98, in both cases the charge for Restores sent to busy agents, with H-MARL's executed actions unchanged step for step. On a supervisory harness, holding interventions until the agent is idle is worth 25.3 and 27.6 points per episode at the published setting. In training, the check decides how a busy step enters the trajectory. Trained without it, KEEP leads at a hundred updates in all four paired seeds and trails from two hundred on in all four. Continued to two thousand updates on three seeds, the repaired recipe ends inside the released interval on one seed and short on two, by 27 and 125 points, a spread across training seeds far wider than the released reproduction interval. Second, the evaluation seeds the environment but not the policy, so a reported mean is one draw, and 88.9% of per-episode outcome variance is the policy's own sampling draw. Third, recovery precision depends on the truth it is scored against. Across five published comparison tables, none states the artifact, sampling, criterion and adversary that would make its numbers comparable. We release the instrument, our patches to both defenders, the traces and checkpoints behind every number, and a five-item disclosure checklist.

title: BODYinTRANSIT-Lab: A Multimodal Dataset for Investigating Sensory-Driven Transformations in Body Perception and Affective Experiences
comments: 18 Pages, 6 Figures, 7 Tables. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Affective Computing
abstract: Multimodal datasets that combine synchronised behavioural and physiological signals with subjective affective and body perception measures are still rare. This limits both the understanding of embodied experience and the development of computational models that infer subjective states from sensor data. We introduce BODYinTRANSIT-Lab, a multimodal dataset that addresses this gap by capturing affective, perceptual, and behavioural responses to the Footsteps Illusion. In this closed-loop paradigm, participants perform walking tasks while receiving real-time manipulated auditory feedback of their own footsteps intended to alter perceived body weight. The dataset comprises synchronised recordings from 101 participants recruited through systematic stratification by eating-disorder symptomatology and physical activity level. BODYinTRANSIT-Lab combines full-body kinematics with electromyography, electrocardiography, respiration, and electrodermal activity. Its annotations capture both immediate and post-trial experience, including within-trial perceived-weight ratings, post-trial assessments of body feelings and affective experience, 3D avatar body visualisations, and quantitative body maps. Psychological, behavioural, demographic, and social measures provide further information about factors that may influence individual responses. We provide a deep learning benchmark that uses walking kinematics to classify relative affective valence and perceived weight within subjects. On within-session, segment-level splits, the baseline model achieved mean balanced accuracies of 45.9% for affective valence and 44.5% for perceived weight. The BODYinTRANSIT-Lab dataset provides an experimentally controlled resource for cognitive neuroscience and affective computing research, with potential applications in affect-aware interactive systems, health and well-being technologies, and creative embodied experiences.

title: CUVE: Making Supervised Classification more Accessible through Visualization
abstract: We present CUVE, an interface that enables people to build classifiers by generating visualizations that are interpretable by both humans and learning algorithms (the Visualization as Intermediate Representation approach). This UI enables users to create supervised classifiers and to visually investigate how to improve them and how they carry out their function. A preliminary study investigates the usability of our prototype and compares it with a traditional text-based programming interface.

title: Continuous 3D Spatial Transcriptomics Reconstruction via Histology-Informed Implicit Neural Representations
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
abstract: Three-dimensional spatial transcriptomics (3D ST) enables the analysis of gene-expression patterns across tissue depths. However, 3D ST measurements are acquired from discrete 2D tissue sections, which are often sparsely sampled due to high acquisition costs. To address this limitation, we propose a histology-informed multi-task implicit neural representation (HIM-INR) for continuous 3D gene-expression reconstruction from sparse ST observations. HIM-INR jointly reconstructs gene-expression profiles and histological representations using an INR with a shared backbone, leveraging densely sampled histological images as auxiliary spatial supervision. Once trained, HIM-INR predicts gene expression at arbitrary 3D coordinates without requiring histological images. Experiments on two 3D ST datasets demonstrate improved reconstruction over existing methods, particularly as the number of missing ST sections increases.

title: Nonadaptive One-Sided Testing of Binary Rank
subjects: Data Structures and Algorithms (cs.DS); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
abstract: The binary rank of a binary matrix is the minimum number of disjoint all-one rectangles that partition its one-entries. We study entry-query testing of binary rank at most $d$, with one-sided error and nonadaptive queries. We give a tester using $\tilde O(d^4/\epsilon^2)$ queries, independent of the matrix dimensions and a general lower bound of $\tilde \Omega(d^{3/2}/\epsilon)$.

title: On Federated Averaging with Partial Participation under a General Variance Condition
subjects: Optimization and Control (math.OC); Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
abstract: In this paper, we study the convergence of Federated Averaging (FedAvg) with partial participation under a general variance condition. In each communication round, the server samples $S$ of the $n$ clients uniformly at random without replacement. The stochastic gradients are assumed to satisfy the so-called ABC condition, which allows their variance to grow with the local objective gaps. For smooth nonconvex objectives, we establish a finite-time stationarity bound in terms of the heterogeneity measure $\sigma_f^\star:=f^\star-\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i^\star$ and the client sampling factor $I_S:=(n-S)/(n-1)$. Here, $f^\star$ and $f_i^\star$ denote the infima of the global average objective and client $i$'s local objective, respectively. The bound exhibits a linear speedup in the number of sampled clients $S$ and recovers the full-participation result when $S=n$. Under diminishing stepsizes, we further prove that the gradient norm converges to zero both in expectation and almost surely. Notably, compared with existing analyses of FedAvg with partial participation, our results require no additional data heterogeneity assumption such as bounded gradient dissimilarity (BGD), and the sampling-induced term in our bound is not amplified by the number of local updates at the leading order. The importance of removing the BGD assumption is illustrated by an example that is smooth and lower bounded but violates BGD, yet is covered by our analysis.

title: Recurrent Modular Structure in Spiking Neural Network Reinforcement Learning
subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Neural and Evolutionary Computing (cs.NE)
abstract: Biological neural circuits are both modular and recurrent, with dense communities sparsely linked to one another. Spiking neural networks (SNNs) for reinforcement learning are usually feed-forward, and it is unclear how to obtain functional modules in a recurrent SNN or what they buy. In this work, we introduce a class of spiking networks, called Community Recurrent SNNs (CoRe SNNs): recurrent networks partitioned into communities with fixed roles. A controller community receives the stimulus, each action has its own community, and latent communities carry internal state. Spiking activity is then a walk between communities, and the action is the community the walk reaches. All learning is local and three-factor, and the recurrent communities are closer to cortical microcircuits than a feed-forward actor. We compare three regimes for obtaining the communities: dynamic modularity, in which a new learning rule we introduce, Map-STDP, encourages modular structure during learning; partial modularity, in which a stochastic block model (SBM) initialization enforces it partly; and full modularity, in which sealing enforces it fully. On CartPole, across three spiking neuron models, Map-STDP improves learning over the same network without it matches full modularity (sealed communities) on two of the three models, and makes the observed spike walk more compressible. Replacing the feed-forward actor of a TD-STDP actor-critic with recurrent action communities improves on the feed-forward network on CartPole and LunarLander, and matches it on Acrobot. How strongly to enforce modularity depends on the task: full modularity helps most on Acrobot, while on LunarLander the dynamic, partial and full regimes perform alike. Overall, these recurrent modular networks can match or even improve upon feed-forward approaches, with improvements in bio-plausibility and energy efficiency.

title: Compositional random forest
abstract: Compositional data have been analysed in the literature from three main points of view: directly on the simplex, in log-ratio coordinates, and as directional data on the unit sphere. In this paper, we construct a random forest framework for compositional responses that accommodates all three. Random forests are ensembles of decision trees, and the split criterion determines how each tree grows. We use the log-likelihood gain as the split criterion and consider distributions defined on the different spaces in which compositions can be represented. The Dirichlet likelihood has been studied in the literature, but its covariance is fixed by its mean up to a single scalar, and its maximum likelihood estimator has no closed form. To obtain more flexible criteria, we use two well-known transformations. First, the square-root transformation maps compositions onto the unit sphere, where existing directional distributions require numerical estimation. We introduce a tangent-normal (TN) distribution, which shares its parameters with the Kent distribution, and construct a split criterion whose gain is computed from additive sufficient statistics: the shape parameters are maximised out in closed form, up to an exponentially small truncation constant, so that no parameter is estimated iteratively. Second, the log-ratio transformation maps compositions to Euclidean space, where the multivariate logistic-normal distribution has a flexible covariance and a closed-form maximum log-likelihood, also based on additive sufficient statistics. Both criteria respond to a shift of the mean, measured relative to the covariance, and to a change in the covariance itself. In simulations, the most accurate forest depended on the covariance structure of the composition. The TN forest was the most accurate in two of the three designs.

title: MammothDP: Private Boosted Decision Trees Ready for Trusted Hardware and Leakage-free Hyperparameters
subjects: Cryptography and Security (cs.CR); Databases (cs.DB); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
abstract: Data spaces like the European Health Data Space (EHDS) require the protection of sensitive data in studies during the data's processing and the study's release alike. In this work, we investigate how to implement this mandate using established trusted execution environments (TEEs) and timing side-channel hardening to protect the processing even under a compromised server, and the state-of-the-art differential privacy (DP) notion to protect the release of studies on tabular data. This combined setup could seem to complete the picture, but in fact raises unexpected security challenges that we mitigate by introducing MammothDP: a significant milestone towards a holistic machine learning system based on the recent gradient boosted decision tree learner S-BDT that is provably DP if used within a privacy filter, timing side-channel hardened, and deployed on a TEE. To achieve a strong privacy-utility tradeoff, we introduce two novel components: an early stopping criterion that adaptively selects the number of trees without any privacy overhead, and an improved rollback protection that is no longer vulnerable under timing side-channel attacks.

title: An Energy-Based Perspective on Machine Learning
abstract: Energy-based models (EBMs) define a distribution through a scalar energy, $p_\theta(x)\propto\exp(-E_\theta(x))$, and are usually presented as one model family among many. This tutorial has a broader goal: beyond introducing EBMs, it uses them as a single lens that connects the different aspects of machine learning. Any EBM is specified by three choices, the energy, which determines what the model represents; the inference procedure, which samples from or optimizes the energy; and the learning method, which fits the energy to data. We first develop these components, including sampling, variational inference, and learning by maximum likelihood, noise contrastive estimation, pseudolikelihood, score matching, and adversarial training, and show that the learning methods share one contrastive structure. We then show that discriminative models, generative models such as GANs, normalizing flows, diffusion and autoregressive models, representation learning methods such as contrastive learning, word2vec, BERT, denoising auto-encoders, and diffusion representations, reinforcement learning with EBM policies and world models, inverse reinforcement learning, and planning, as well as inference-time computation with verifiers, are all EBMs that differ in these three choices, mostly in how they handle the partition function and sampling. This view explains existing methods, organizes them into a common framework, and suggests new algorithms by replacing one component while keeping the others, with composition of energies as a principled way to combine learned models at inference time.

title: Exploring Post-Hoc Disentanglement of Audio Foundation Models for Music Similarity
abstract: Audio foundation models like CLAP, MuQ, and MERT excel at capturing general musical similarity. On the other hand, their entangled latent spaces limit interpretability and fine-grained attribute control. Conditional Similarity Networks (CSN) address this by pairing a backbone representation model with learned masks that gate the embedding space into attribute-specific subspaces. However, existing methods train the backbone from scratch, rather than leveraging pretrained foundation models. We instead present a systematic study of post-hoc disentanglement, adapting CSN to gate frozen pretrained embeddings. We evaluate adding trainable parameters to adapt the embedding under different masking and pooling regimes across two datasets. Our findings show that minimal adaptation capacity is sufficient for post-hoc gating to improve both attribute-specific disentanglement and overall retrieval performance, while pooling, masking, and depth choices yield limited additional gains.

title: UGG: Unified Generative Geometry Model
comments: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 31 pages, 7 figures, 6 tables. Project page: this https URL
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract: Understanding 4D scenes is a core challenge in visual intelligence, requiring models to jointly capture scene geometry, appearance, and dynamics from partial observations. However, existing approaches are subdivided into feedforward models for direct geometric prediction, and generative models for visual synthesis. We introduce UGG, a unified framework for 4D scene understanding that jointly models RGB video and geometric representations such as depth and camera pose. By assigning different noise levels across modalities and time, UGG formulates visual generation and geometric prediction as conditional completion within a single generative model. This flexible formulation enables the model to learn from diverse, heterogeneous datasets with different subsets of geometric and visual annotations. Furthermore, our generative formulation enables inference-time search over multiple plausible scene hypotheses, using geometric evidence extracted from observed RGB frames to improve geometric prediction without ground truth geometry. We demonstrate UGG's effectiveness over non-unified baselines across camera-controlled video generation, depth estimation, and camera pose prediction, including in challenging sparse observation settings. Code and visualizations are available at this https URL

title: A Theory of Cross-Validation Variance
comments: 27 pages main text, 57 pages supplementary material with 6 sections, 1 figure
subjects: Machine Learning (stat.ML); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Statistics Theory (math.ST)
abstract: Cross-validation estimates predictive performance by repeatedly splitting the data into training and validation sets, fitting the model on the first and evaluating it on the second. Every observation influences the estimate in two roles, through its own evaluation when it is held out and through the models it helps fit when it trains. The random splits determine its weight in each role. From this representation, we prove an exact finite-sample identity for the variance of the cross-validated estimate. For a given splitting scheme with a common training set size, the variance is a function of these weights, with constants of the model, the metric, and the population. It covers metrics averaged over observations, such as mean squared error, and over case--control pairs, such as the AUC. The identity shows which schemes to use. The variance decomposes into sampling variance, which depends only on the training size, and variance due to the random fold splitting, which arises when the weights change from one draw of the splits to the next. K-fold cross-validation, whose weights are equal across observations by design, is therefore variance optimal at first order; Monte Carlo and bootstrap cross-validation are not. The first-order variance of K-fold does not depend on K, and under reasonable conditions on the model leave-one-out has the smallest variance of any K-fold scheme. For the AUC the same holds for leave-pair-out, which evaluates every case--control pair. Finally, we show the cross-validated estimate is asymptotically normal with the identity's full variance. Together, these results provide a general theoretical foundation for inference on cross-validated performance and establish principles for selecting variance-optimal cross-validation designs.

title: Bayesian inverse problems and epidemic-threshold uncertainty for a heterogeneous SIS reaction-diffusion model
subjects: Analysis of PDEs (math.AP); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Number Theory (math.NT); Statistics Theory (math.ST); Populations and Evolution (q-bio.PE)
abstract: We study Bayesian inference of persistence from early observations of a heterogeneous susceptible--infected--susceptible (SIS) reaction--diffusion model with standard incidence. We show that the leading prevalence dynamics depend on the unknown coefficients only through the difference between the transmission and recovery rates and the infected diffusivity. The same pair determines the principal eigenvalue whose sign governs persistence, so early prevalence can inform the threshold even when the individual rates remain uncertain. We prove global weak well-posedness and quantitative parameter stability for the SIS system and use the resulting observation-map estimates to establish Bayesian well-posedness. For an initial infection of size $\varepsilon$, we derive a uniform second-order expansion that describes how the separate rates enter prevalence. Incidence depends explicitly on transmission at leading order. When the noise standard deviation is proportional to $\varepsilon$, we prove $O(\varepsilon)$ convergence in Hellinger distance of the nonlinear posteriors to their low-prevalence limits for both prevalence alone and joint prevalence and incidence data. We bound the principal eigenvalue using the growth rate of the infected $L^2$ norm between two times. This rate gives a lower bound for the full nonlinear system, and the upper bound separates spatial transients from nonlinear saturation. Uniform spectral estimates and bounds on infection size and measurement error give sufficient conditions for persistence and extinction. We also bound the error in posterior persistence probabilities under forward and eigenvalue approximation, accounting for posterior mass near the threshold. Numerical examples illustrate threshold inference and the predicted \(O(\varepsilon)\) convergence of the nonlinear posteriors to their low-prevalence limits in Hellinger distance.

title: ReTrace: Distilling Tool-Using Agents into Planner-Free Workflows
subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Multiagent Systems (cs.MA)
abstract: Business process automation runs the same Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) again and again on new inputs. Large Language Model (LLM) agents can follow an SOP written in natural language, but they call an LLM to choose every step of every run, which adds latency and cost at scale. We present ReTrace, which turns an SOP and a few logged agent runs into a reusable workflow in which code, not an LLM, selects the next step. The agent's reasoning, the explanation it writes with each tool call, often states why it took an action; the tool calls alone do not. ReTrace extracts the condition behind each step, merges these conditions across runs into a compact rule document, and generates an executable workflow from it. Only this last stage depends on the platform, so rule documents can be compiled for different orchestration platforms. On $79$ procedures from our production platform, ReTrace workflows reach $93.8\%$ completion, against $96.8\%$ for the agent, at $24\%$ lower cost per task. On $\tau^2$-Bench, they reach $75.8\%$ task success (agent: $80.6\%$) and run in $1.3$s instead of $170$s; three rounds of repair on training failures lift $k{=}2$ workflows from $66.7\%$ to $81.2\%$. On eight SOP-Bench procedures, ReTrace without repair trails few-shot generation ($80.6\%$ vs. $83.6\%$), but repair from labeled training failures lifts it to $87.8\%$ at $0.40$s per task, compared to $85.5\%$ in $46.6$s for the agent.

title: Contrastive Discovery: Open-Ended Scientific Discovery over Competing Explanations
comments: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 55 pages. Project page: this https URL
subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computation and Language (cs.CL); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
abstract: LLM agents are increasingly used for open-ended, data-driven scientific discovery, yet most of them evaluate hypotheses pointwise, testing an empirical claim $h$ only against its complement $\neg h$. When evidence rejects $h$, the agent learns that one explanation is unlikely but not which alternative the evidence supports. To recover that alternative, we introduce Contrastive Discovery, which replaces the single hypothesis with a contrast set, a scientific question paired with mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive competing explanations. Each experiment is scored by how its evidence redistributes belief across the set, and the question is resolved when belief concentrates on one explanation. Because contrast sets change only the unit an agent proposes and scores, an existing agent can use them to re-evaluate evidence it has already collected or to guide its search. Across six domains, $89\%$ of the pointwise candidates with the largest belief shifts are rejections. On the same evidence, contrast sets resolve $73\%$ of these candidates to a specific alternative. When contrast sets guide search, the agent resolves $67\%$ more questions than pointwise surprisal under the same experiment budget. In a blinded study, $38$ human experts chose the same explanation on $78\%$ of resolved questions and on $82\%$ of questions where the pointwise agent rejected its hypothesis and stopped. Together, these results support explicit competing explanations as a way for discovery agents to resolve more scientific questions from the same evidence and validation budget.
